title: Oklahoma native Blake Griffin says taxpayers had little choice on $900 million Thunder arena
content:
In December 2023, 71 percent of voters in Oklahoma City approved a one-percent sales tax over six years, with the money going into an arena facility sales tax to build a new home to keep the Thunder in the city. That ended up costing taxpayers at least $850 million, while Oklahoma City’s ownership group, led by Clay Bennett, will pitch in $50 million. In exchange, the franchise committed to remaining in the city through at least 2050.

To Blake Griffin, a native Oklahoman, the voters agreed to foot the large bill because, as he put it in the opening monologue of his late-night show, “What choice do fans really have?”

On this week’s episode of “The Stepback with Blake Griffin” on Prime, the former All-Star highlighted a quote from professor J.C. Bradbury of Kennesaw State University, who has studied public policy toward arena and stadium construction.

“Whoever negotiated this for the city of Oklahoma City should be fired for incompetence,” Bradbury told the Associated Press at the time of the initial vote. “It is by far the worst stadium deal I’ve ever seen negotiated from a public standpoint.”

“They know that the alternative is to lose the team and watch Shai (Gilgeous-Alexander) play basketball for the Wichita Thunder,” Griffin quipped before noting that “Oklahoma City has the Thunder because Seattle refused to build the Sonics a new arena.”

The Seattle SuperSonics moved to Oklahoma City on July 2, 2008, after 41 years of NBA basketball in the Pacific Northwest.

Despite acknowledging how “super exciting” it was for the Thunder to come to his home city, Griffin mused that taxpayer dollars could go to other essential uses like starting teacher pay, which he said ranks 45th in the country. Both of his parents were teachers, he noted.

“Fans feel hamstrung having to pay billions of dollars to keep the teams they love,” Griffin said.

In March, the Thunder broke ground on its new Continental Coliseum. It will replace the 24-year-old Paycom Center in 2028.

“This moment speaks to our aspirations as a city,” Mayor David Holt said at the time. “Not only are we making the statement that we wish to remain a big league city; the scale and beauty of this project also makes an aesthetic statement that will resonate for generations. This is the city’s most ambitious public project in our history.”

Bennett praised the fans who agreed to pay for the franchise’s future.

“In 2026, we’re building a modern American downtown. What an incredible opportunity and special gift,” the Thunder’s chairman said in March. “This belongs to every citizen who voted yes to make this possible. This is your day. This is your building, and we are forever grateful.”

On Nov. 12, Holt posted renderings of the arena’s future look, saying it will not only keep the Thunder in the city past 2053, but it will also improve its ability to recruit major concerts.

“This beautiful building will be among the finest arenas in the world, and it will raise the architectural bar for OKC,” Holt wrote.

The vote’s stipulations state that if costs exceed the original estimate, taxpayers will be responsible for the difference, as Bennett is committed to no more than $50 million. Holt has already noted that the arena cost could be up to $1 billion.

Griffin, born on March 16, 1989, grew up in Oklahoma City. By the Thunder’s inaugural 2008-09 NBA season, Griffin was already a dominant college sophomore at the University of Oklahoma. He was named the Naismith Men’s College Basketball Player of the Year and became the No. 1 pick to the LA Clippers.

Since moving to Oklahoma, the Thunder are tied with the Golden State Warriors for the most Western Conference finals appearances, with six. The city has seen three players (Kevin Durant, Russell Westbrook, Shai Gilgeous-Alexander) win the league’s MVP in the Paycom Center. They’ve made two NBA Finals appearances and won a title in 2025.
